correctness.rationale: For finite p != 2, the explicit two-coordinate family x=(1,0), y=(b,1) has continuous denominator D_p. For p>2, D_p(0)>0 and D_p(-1)<0; at a boundary zero b_p in (-1,0), the numerator is strictly positive because 1-b_p > 1+b_p. Approaching from the D_p>0 side makes the quotient tend to +infinity. For 1<=p<2, D_p(0)<0 and D_p(1)>0; at a boundary zero b_p in (0,1), the numerator is strictly negative, so approach from the D_p<0 side again gives +infinity. For p=infinity the denominator is 2-(1-b)^2 and the numerator is 1, with the zero b=1-sqrt(2). For p=2, the parallelogram identity makes every admissible quotient exactly -1. Two-coordinate embedding transfers unboundedness from ell_p^2 to every ell_p(I) with at least two coordinates.
risks: The value +infinity is an extended-real description of an unbounded supremum, not an attained quotient.
The checker samples exponents; the universal classification relies on the analytic sign proof, not numerical enumeration.

originality.rationale: The defining 2023 article was inspected throughout its P(X) section, including Definition 3.1, the normalized form, the Hilbert characterization, lower bounds, and its sequence-space discussion. No upper-finiteness theorem or exact ell_p dichotomy was found. Searches covered the exact notation, Pythagorean orthogonality, ell_p aliases, and unbounded/infinite-supremum language. The closest same-invariant prior finding is a single regular-octagonal unbounded example; the closest ell_p findings use different invariants. Thus neither title similarity nor a special-case divergence result implies the accepted all-p classification.

value.rationale: The result settles the basic finiteness question for the defining invariant on the canonical ell_p scale. It shows a sharp qualitative phase transition: the quotient is finite only at the Hilbert exponent and is unbounded at every other p, including all smooth uniformly convex non-Hilbert ell_p spaces. This demonstrates that divergence is intrinsic to the quotient's denominator geometry rather than a corner phenomenon of polyhedral norms, and it materially changes how P(X) can be used as a numerical geometric constant.
risks: The finding is a finiteness classification for one standard scale, not a general characterization of all Banach spaces with finite P(X).
